item.title: Iran's president says peace MoU with U.S. in interests of Tehran
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-30
Iran's president says peace MoU with U.S. in interests of Tehran TEHRAN, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Saturday the peace memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed between Iran and the United States is in the interests of the country, West Asia and the world. During a ceremony in the Iranian capital Tehran, he stressed that with the MoU's implementation, the United States and Israel will not be able to cause chaos, aggression and insecurity in the region, and regional states will be able to pursue the path of stability and development, according to a statement published on the website of his office. Pezeshkian highlighted the need for foiling the "enemies' sinister plots" through promoting unity and solidarity among Muslim states. He said that Iran has never been the party to start a war, adding, "We do not welcome war, but will stand strongly against any aggressor, and no power can force a nation that is standing with all its might and will into surrender." Also on Saturday, Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi warned in a social media post that "major" efforts are underway to manipulate global energy markets for personal gains and prolong the U.S. war against Iran. Separately, Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps announced on the same day that the country's security forces have dealt a "decisive" blow to a "terrorist" team affiliated with the United States and Israel in southeastern Sistan and Baluchestan province, killing one of its members and arresting six others. On Feb. 28, Israel and the United States launched joint attacks on Tehran and other Iranian cities. Iran responded with waves of missile and drone attacks targeting Israel and U.S. bases and assets in the region, and tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz. On June 18, the United States and Iran signed the MoU on ending the war in the region on all fronts. Under the MoU, they were scheduled to hold negotiations within a period of 60 days, which ended on Aug. 17, to reach a final agreement, but the talks' fate remains unclear following the escalation between the two countries last month. item.title: Kyrgyz youth on China: The country we see
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-30
Kyrgyz youth on China: The country we see Young people from the Confucius Institute at Bishkek State University read the poem "To the Oak Tree" in Chinese. (People's Daily Online/Chu Mengqi) China and Kyrgyzstan share a long border and an even longer friendship. In the past few years that friendship has quickened. Chinese classrooms in Bishkek fill early. Confucius Institutes stay noisy after dark. Young Kyrgyz students are learning not only the language, but a country that no longer feels distant or abstract. Five of them, all from the Confucius Institute at Bishkek State University, talk about how China entered their lives. Batyrkanova Kanykei Batyrkanova Kanykei, student at the Confucius Institute at Bishkek State University. (People's Daily Online/Chu Mengqi) Batyrkanova Kanykei got her Chinese name Yang Yaning from her teacher. She disliked it at first. The characters looked cramped to her, "like a little mountain." Five years later she uses the name without thinking about it. Chinese friends tell her it sounds lovely, and she can answer them in Chinese. "I grew into it," she says, "The name, the language, and then China." She had not meant to study Chinese. Her uncle told her that the two countries were drawing closer and that the language would matter for work. She is glad she listened. As her feelings for the language changed, so did Bishkek. When she started university, there were only a couple of Chinese restaurants. Now she can find Sichuan food, Zhejiang dishes, Peking duck. One afternoon she followed the smell of hotpot down the stairs of her building and knocked. The neighbor was Chinese. She reads Chinese web novels, follows comics, and spends her free time on Chinese apps and television. She would like to subtitle more of those shows for people in Kyrgyzstan. She would also like her Chinese friends to visit her world: a yurt, a horse, the pace of a family that still knows the steppe. She hopes to work in an embassy. "That seems like a place where I can build a cultural bridge that brings our people together." Beishekeeva Nurisa Beishekeeva Nurisa (second from left), student at the Confucius Institute at Bishkek State University. (People's Daily Online/Chu Mengqi) Beishekeeva Nurisa's Kyrgyz name means sun. Her teacher called her Yangyang. A few years ago she chose Chinese out of curiosity. This September she will begin a master's degree at Zhejiang University to study international Chinese language education. Shanghai was her first stop in China, and she was impressed by its international and modern atmosphere. After studying there and coming home, she found Bishkek different: more Chinese visitors, more shops, new restaurants and supermarkets. "You can meet Chinese people at the bank and in the mall." Many of the electric cars in the city are Chinese. "Families can afford them. They're clean, and people like driving them." Learning the language, she says, meant learning how people live. She was pleased when Bishkek screened Chinese films, because a film can explain a country's habits more quickly than a classroom can. "I want to make contributions to such cultural exchanges, offering opportunities for our people to better appreciate each other." Kanyshai Zhakhanshaeva Kanyshai Zhakhanshaeva, student at the Confucius Institute at Bishkek State University. (People's Daily Online/Chu Mengqi) Kanyshai Zhakhanshaeva has studied Chinese for four years. She chose it because China felt impossible to ignore, and because the language would help her work and study. She listens to Jay Chou, especially his song "Blue and White Porcelain." Chinese social media platforms WeChat and Xiaohongshu are part of her day; so are Chinese e-commerce platforms like Pinduoduo. Most of the parcels are small: pens, stickers, things for a desk. She has also watched the larger change around her, in trade, in classrooms, and in the number of people moving between the two countries. She wants to work as a translator, to help the relationship between the two nations keep moving. Zhyrgalbaev Kanybek Zhyrgalbaev Kanybek (second from right), student at the Confucius Institute at Bishkek State University. (People's Daily Online/Chu Mengqi) Zhyrgalbaev Kanybek's Chinese teacher named him Xue Pei. He has a keen interest in traditional Chinese culture. He loves calligraphy and can recite "Invitation to Wine" by Tang poet Li Bai. "Chinese calligraphy is fascinating," he says. "There is always another style." In Bishkek, Chinese cars and goods have become an ordinary sight. Shopping on Chinese e-commerce platforms, a rarity only a few years ago, has become a part of everyday life. "If you order something, it can be here in two weeks." He wants to become a translator whose work carries real strength—the kind that takes meaning from one language and sets it down in another. Almazbek Kyzy Umut Almazbek Kyzy Umut, student at the Confucius Institute at Bishkek State University. (People's Daily Online/Chu Mengqi) "I didn't want to learn Chinese. It looked too hard," Almazbek Kyzy Umut says frankly. Her father said the language would matter, so she chose Chinese as her major, struggled, and then found she liked it. Last year, she made it to the global finals of the "Chinese Bridge" Chinese language proficiency competition and visited Beijing, Nanping, Fuzhou, Quanzhou and other places in China. This year she has been to Guangzhou, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Shanghai and Zhangjiajie. Of all the cities, Chengdu is her favorite. "People there know how to enjoy life. They love taking walks and dancing, and the architecture is also fascinating. Guangzhou and Shanghai have a fast‑paced vibe, but in Chengdu you can unwind and feel completely at ease." She believes China‑Kyrgyzstan relations will keep getting better. "There are abundant opportunities for both friendly cooperation and economic and trade exchanges." After travelling across many cities in China, she is more convinced that to understand a language is to draw closer to a country. She hopes to bring home what she has seen and felt on her journey, and share stories of her homeland with more Chinese friends. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Bishkek, where China feels close at hand
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-30
Bishkek, where China feels close at hand Chinese drink brand Mixue has become the fashionable drink of choice among young people in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. (People's Daily Online/Chu Mengqi) Walk into Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, and Chinese elements are already woven into the city. At Mixue, a Chinese drink brand, young people enjoy bubble tea cheerfully. On the road, electric taxis and buses made in China move through the streets. In an underground mall, HSK textbooks sit on shelves; young people stop to turn the pages. When locals meet Chinese visitors, greetings such as "ni hao," "xie xie," and "zai jian" roll off their tongues more easily than before. Ablaisov has driven a BYD taxi for two years. (People's Daily Online/Kou Jie) Ablaisov, a local taxi driver, has driven a BYD taxi for two years. "Chinese new energy vehicles are environmentally sound and efficient, and the price is reasonable," he says. "People here recognize their quality. A Chinese car is now regarded as a high-end product." Growing numbers of Chinese-made electric buses have also entered regular service. Drivers find the vehicles simple to operate and comfortable to ride, and passengers have responded positively. The same presence fills the shopping centers. From smartphones to household appliances, Chinese goods occupy the shelves, and the brands are already familiar. Back at Mixue, Chinese fruit teas remain the most popular drinks, and regular customers return each day. Nearby, Chinese restaurants stay crowded. Xinjiang-style big-plate chicken has become a dish many locals order with genuine liking. HSK Chinese textbooks sit on shelves in Bishkek's underground malls. (People's Daily Online/Kou Jie) Chinese e-commerce is changing how people shop as well. Kanyshai Zhakhanshaeva, who is studying Chinese, often browses Chinese e-commerce platforms for small stationery she likes and has become a loyal buyer of Chinese products. Zhyrgalbaev Kanybek, also learning the language, notes that the two countries are not far apart. Goods arrive in about two weeks; prices are fair and quality is reliable, so many people here use Chinese platforms. Phone cases, small appliances, clothes, toys—a single parcel crosses mountains and rivers and draws two ordinary lives closer together. Behind the flow of goods, language and culture are taking root. At the Confucius Institute of Bishkek State University, more young people are studying Chinese. Classrooms echo with the sound of students reading aloud; shelves are lined with textbooks and books on Chinese culture. As exchanges between China and Kyrgyzstan grow closer, more local young people are taking up Chinese. (People's Daily Online/Chu Mengqi) Batyrkanova Kanykei and Almazbek Kyzy Umut are both students at the university. Kanykei has studied Chinese for five years. In high school she read Chinese web novels and comics, and that reading grew into a lasting interest in Chinese culture. She now follows many Chinese social media platforms like Xiaohongshu and shops on e-commerce platforms like Taobao, encountering everyday Chinese life through the internet. Umut competed in the global finals of the "Chinese Bridge" Chinese Proficiency Competition last year and visited Beijing, Nanping, Fuzhou, and Quanzhou in China. This year she traveled to Guangzhou, Chengdu, Shenzhen, Shanghai, and Zhangjiajie. Of those cities, Chengdu left the strongest impression. "People there know how to enjoy life. In Chengdu you can unwind and feel completely at ease." Sadygaliev Uran, associate professor at the Kyrgyz-Chinese Faculty at Bishkek State University, places the present in a longer history. "The foundation of China–Kyrgyzstan relations can be traced to the ancient Silk Road, and later to the Belt and Road Initiative. From the thousand-year ruins of the ancient city of Suyab to the classrooms of the Confucius Institute, the cultural exchanges between the two countries has continued for centuries." These ties also create practical opportunities for young people. Orozbek, 29, works as a translator at Yutong Bus Co., a leading Chinese bus manufacturer, and has studied Chinese for five and a half years. After he took the position, his younger siblings became interested in Chinese and began to study it. Many of his friends now do business with China. "A great deal of Chinese merchandise is coming in. The market is huge." From a cup of Mixue milk tea to the electric buses on the street, from cross-border parcels to Chinese-language classes at the Confucius Institute, the friendship between China and Kyrgyzstan is visible in ordinary life in Bishkek. The ancient Silk Road is gaining fresh vitality, witnessing the steady strides of the two peoples walking forward together. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Chinese FM holds phone talks with Nepali counterpart
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-30
Chinese FM holds phone talks with Nepali counterpart BEIJING, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's package of assistance to Nepal is being implemented, including emergency cash assistance and humanitarian aid, with some relief supplies set to arrive in Kathmandu soon, said Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi during his phone conversation with Nepali Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal on Saturday. Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, said that a severe mudslide disaster, triggered by a sudden glacier collapse in Nepal's border area, has caused significant casualties and left people missing on both sides. It has been the most serious cross-border disaster between the two countries in recent years, and the relief efforts are unprecedentedly complex and arduous. He said that China attaches great importance to the situation. Chinese President Xi Jinping immediately issued important instructions, setting clear requirements for rescue and emergency response work. Chinese Premier Li Qiang traveled to the disaster-hit area to guide the work on the ground. Wang said that while urgently carrying out rescue and relief efforts on its own side, China extended a helping hand at the earliest opportunity and supported Nepal in its emergency disaster relief efforts. Xi has sent a condolence message to Nepali President Ram Chandra Poudel, and Li has expressed condolences to Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah, Wang noted. China will provide emergency aid to the disaster-hit area in Nepal and carry out international rescue cooperation, according to a meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee. This is an important political decision made by China and demonstrates China's friendship with Nepal, he said. Wang said that two teams of Chinese tunnel rescue experts had rushed to the disaster-stricken area and Kathmandu to offer assistance, and China has shared with Nepal important information such as images, satellite and hydrological data of the disaster-stricken area, including early warning information of the upstream barrier lake. He said that for Nepalese citizens stranded on the Chinese side, China has made proper arrangements and will assist them in returning to Nepal as soon as possible, expressing his gratitude and hope that Nepal will continue to assist and transfer Chinese citizens in Nepal. Wang said that China and Nepal are a community linked by mountains and rivers and sharing a common destiny. In the face of the disaster, the two countries should stand together firmly, join hands to deal with it and overcome the difficulties together, and interpret the traditional friendship across the Himalayas with concrete actions. Shisir conveyed condolences from Nepali leaders to the Chinese government and people and to the families of the victims, and expressed sincere gratitude for China's emergency humanitarian assistance. He said that although both Nepal and China had been hit by the disaster, China had overcome its own difficulties to extend condolences and provide assistance to Nepal at the earliest opportunity, fully demonstrating the high level of Nepal-China relations. The Nepali side once again expressed its gratitude to China and will continue to work closely with China to make every effort to rescue Chinese nationals who remain stranded or unaccounted for, while jointly working to locate and rescue missing foreign nationals, he said. Nepal stands ready to strengthen cooperation with China in areas such as post-disaster reconstruction, disaster prevention and mitigation, and climate change response, and to further advance the strategic partnership of cooperation between the two countries, he said. item.title: How the SCO is raising the bar for better global governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-30
How the SCO is raising the bar for better global governance BEIJING, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- The world is facing a growing crisis of global governance. Protectionism, unilateralism and power politics are throttling international cooperation just as mounting global challenges demand it most. Against this backdrop, Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at last year's "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" Meeting, calling for a more just and equitable system of global governance. The SCO offers a practical answer. Over the past 25 years, it has demonstrated how countries with different political systems, development paths and civilizations can work together. Guided by the Shanghai Spirit of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations and pursuit of common development, the SCO's 25-year practice offers a vivid illustration of the five principles of the Global Governance Initiative -- adhering to sovereign equality, abiding by international rule of law, practicing multilateralism, advocating the people-centered approach, and focusing on taking real actions. These principles are reflected in the SCO's increasingly institutionalized cooperation across a wide range of sectors. With regional security and stability at the heart of its original mission, SCO countries have committed themselves to long-term good neighborliness, friendship and cooperation based on equality, consultation and respect for diversity. The establishment of four new security-focused centers demonstrated the SCO's emphasis on translating multilateral consensus into concrete action. Cooperation among SCO countries has helped thwart more than 1,400 terrorism- and extremism-related incidents in the past 25 years, while the organization has conducted over 40 joint counter-terrorism exercises and operations. The SCO's approach to security also reflects a broader understanding among SCO countries that lasting security cannot be separated from political trust, economic development and people-to-people exchanges. The launch of seven China-SCO cooperation platforms covering green industry, digital economy, scientific and technological innovation, energy, higher education, vocational and technical education, and artificial intelligence further underscores the emphasis on shared development with people-centered outcomes. Through high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and closer alignment of development strategies, SCO members have seen positive momentum in both foreign trade and intra-SCO commerce. Calculations based on World Trade Organization data showed the total volume of goods imports and exports of the ten members reached about 8.88 trillion U.S. dollars in 2025. Projects such as the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, the Silk Road e-commerce service hub and the SCO university network are further turning connectivity into tangible benefits, making it easier for people across SCO countries to travel, trade, study and access broader economic opportunities. People-to-people exchange activities have also become an important pillar of SCO cooperation. Through institutionalized dialogue and expanded interaction, differences in history, culture and civilization can be turned into sources of mutual understanding and cooperation. Beyond the region, the SCO has played an active role in upholding the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and international law, contributing to the settlement of regional and international issues and promoting coordination among multilateral mechanisms. The SCO Plus format has further broadened the space for dialogue among the Global South, facilitating exchanges in governance experience and practical cooperation. Over the past decades, the SCO has shown that diversity need not lead to division, and that countries with different political systems, development paths, and civilizations can cooperate on equal footing without butting heads. Looking ahead, the SCO is well positioned to bolster high-quality regional development and contribute more wisdom to building a more just and equitable global governance system. item.title: Seven years on, revisiting President Xi's signed article published in Kyrgyzstan
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-30
Seven years on, revisiting President Xi's signed article published in Kyrgyzstan
Chinese President Xi Jinping on Aug. 28 published a signed article titled "Jointly Opening up New Prospects for the High-Quality Development of China-Kyrgyzstan Relations" in the Slovo Kyrgyzstana and the Kabar National News Agency ahead of his arrival in Kyrgyzstan for a state visit and attendance at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026 in Bishkek. The article pointed out that China and Kyrgyzstan are good neighbors sharing weal and woe, good partners with a shared future, and good friends who help each other succeed. Seven years ago, in June 2019, before his state visit to Kyrgyzstan, President Xi published a signed article in local media titled "May China-Kyrgyzstan Friendship Thrive Like an Evergreen Tree." Seven years on, how have the aspirations laid out in the article reverberated across Bishkek?
(Web editor: Peng Yukai, Wu Chengliang)

item.title: Xi says China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation entering "golden period" of rapid development
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-30
Xi says China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation entering "golden period" of rapid development BISHKEK, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- The China-Kyrgyzstan cooperation has ushered in a "golden period" of rapid development, Chinese President Xi Jinping said on Sunday as he landed here for the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026 and a state visit to Kyrgyzstan. Upon the arrival, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov and his wife welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the Manas International Airport. In a written speech, Xi extended sincere greetings and best wishes to Japarov and the people of Kyrgyzstan on behalf of the Chinese government and people. Noting that China and Kyrgyzstan share a time-honored traditional friendship, Xi said that the majestic Tianshan Mountains stands as witnesses to the millennia of friendly exchanges between their peoples. Over the 34 years since the establishment of diplomatic relations, the China-Kyrgyzstan relationship has withstood the test of a changing international landscape, maintained sound and stable development throughout, and reached the high level of a comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era. In recent years, bilateral trade volume and people-to-people exchanges have reached new highs, Xi said, noting that major projects including the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway have been successfully implemented, and the tangible results of mutually beneficial cooperation have broadly benefited the two peoples. Xi said that during the visit he will have in-depth exchanges of views with Japarov on China-Kyrgyzstan relations, cooperation in various fields between the two countries, and international and regional issues of common concern, and draw a new blueprint for building a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future. "I look forward to attending the SCO Bishkek Summit, working with all parties to revisit the 25-year development experience of the SCO, jointly discuss cooperation plans, create the future of the organization, and promote the continuous new development of the organization," Xi said. item.title: China helps SCO evolve into comprehensive cooperation platform, says Tajik economist
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-29
China helps SCO evolve into comprehensive cooperation platform, says Tajik economist This photo taken on Aug. 30, 2025 shows an exterior view of the main venue of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2025 in north China's Tianjin. (Xinhua/Sun Fanyue) DUSHANBE, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- China is helping transform the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) from a security-focused regional body into a comprehensive platform -- one spanning economy, technology, transport and finance, a Tajik economist said. In an interview with Xinhua, Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University, described China's 2024-2025 rotating presidency as one of the most productive periods in the SCO history. During its presidency, China hosted over 200 events, issued 92 outcome documents, and put forward 36 major cooperation initiatives, Ulmasov noted. "The SCO has gone beyond being solely a regional platform and is gaining global significance." China has become one of SCO's primary economic engines, said Ulmasov, highlighting SCO leaders' approval of a development strategy for the organization in the 2026-2035 period and the member states' decision to establish an SCO development bank at the SCO summit held last year in China's port city of Tianjin. These measures are particularly important for Central Asia, where there is significant demand for financing in transport, energy, water management and digital infrastructure, he said, noting that once the bank becomes fully operational, it could provide countries in the region with new sources of long-term financing. On the logistics front, Ulmasov said that Belt and Road cooperation on infrastructure is fostering closer transport, trade and logistics links among SCO member states, particularly in Central Asia. New cross-border routes are transforming Central Asia from a landlocked area in the Eurasian transport grid into a dynamic hub connecting East and West, as well as North and South, he said. Young students from the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) countries perform during the Kaleidoscope Cultural Bazaar in north China's Tianjin, Aug. 6, 2025. (Xinhua/Li Ran) The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway could also become a new driver of regional economic development, said the Tajik expert. The project is designed to create a new land route connecting China and Central Asia and shorten the existing China-Europe route by about 900 km, providing an alternative to traditional transport routes. Looking ahead, Ulmasov said the SCO is embarking on a new development stage with cooperation expanding beyond traditional trade, transport and conventional energy to technological modernization in green energy, artificial intelligence, the digital economy and emerging industries. China is aligning its own modernization drive with the development needs of fellow SCO member states, creating a new model of cooperation that combines Chinese technology, local resources, joint production and access to regional markets, he said. China, he said, is offering SCO members more than a share in its economic momentum; it is offering a way into the high-tech supply chains of the future. As these initiatives take root, he added, the SCO could become a premier hub for the region's green and digital economic transformation. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.
